title: The Perfect Portrait
premise: Oscar Crane, an insurance investigator whose photographic memory has quietly exposed three 'accidents' as murders, is hired by a nervous widow, Vivian Ashford, to prove that her husband's death was natural — before it happens. The retainer is dated a week in the future, and the husband, gallery owner Edmund Ashford, is very much alive. Digging into the Ashford estate, Oscar uncovers a thirty-year-old forgery ring: a stolen Vermeer replaced by a perfect copy, and four partners bound by silence, one of whom has begun eliminating the others. As Oscar races the killer through alibis built decades ago, he realizes his own memory of a childhood fire — the one that killed his parents and left him with his uncanny recall — is tangled in the same conspiracy. In the end, Oscar exposes the surviving forger, Edmund himself, who staged his own death to escape his partners' debts; justice arrives outside the law when Vivian, learning the truth, chooses to let him vanish rather than face trial, and Oscar burns the only photograph that could convict her.
about_author: Kestrel Sandoval is the pen name of a former forensic archivist who spent a decade cataloguing disputed artworks for European insurers before turning to fiction. They live off-grid on the Atlantic coast, where they restore antique cameras and write mysteries about memory, money, and the lies people preserve like paintings.

chapters.title: The Retainer
chapters.summary: Oscar Crane, POV. A client named Vivian Ashford pays Oscar a generous retainer to prove her husband's death will be natural — dated six days from now. Oscar's photographic memory flags the impossible date immediately. The emotional beat is cold curiosity sharpening into unease: he takes the case because the wrongness of it itches like a misfiled document.

chapters.title: A Man Very Much Alive
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. Surveillance confirms Edmund Ashford, gallery owner, is alive and oblivious. Oscar interviews the household staff and memorizes every inconsistency: a locked attic, a burned ledger smell, a servant who flinches at the word 'Vermeer.' The beat is mounting disorientation — Oscar is investigating a murder that hasn't happened yet.

chapters.title: Three Accidents
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV, flashback-woven. We learn how Oscar solved three deaths the police called accidents, and why he works alone and invisible. His method: total recall of detail no witness can fake. The emotional beat is guarded pride shadowed by loneliness — being right has cost him every friend he had.

chapters.title: The Widow's Hands
chapters.summary: Vivian, POV. Vivian rehearses her grief in advance, practicing tears in a mirror while Edmund sleeps downstairs. She knows more than she told Oscar. The beat is chilling complicity — she may be protecting her husband, or preparing to bury him.

chapters.title: The Attic Ledger
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. Breaking into the Ashford attic, Oscar finds a half-burned ledger listing four names and dates spanning thirty years — two already dead in 'accidents' matching his old cases. The beat is vertigo: the deaths he solved were chapters of a longer book, and someone is still writing it.

chapters.title: Partners in Paint
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. Research reveals the four names: 1994 art-school friends who bought a stolen Vermeer together, sold the original, and displayed a forgery ever since. Each partner held a piece of the proof. The beat is dawning scale — this isn't a murder plot, it's a slow demolition of witnesses.

chapters.title: Alibi, Thirty Years Old
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. He reconstructs the night of the theft from weather records, train timetables, and a single photograph, finding that every partner's alibi depends on the others staying silent. The beat is intellectual exhilaration curdling into dread as he sees how neatly the machine was built.

chapters.title: What the Fire Left
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. A name in the ledger matches the insurance file from the fire that killed Oscar's parents — the fire that gave him his memory and took his childhood. The beat is personal rupture: this case was never random; the past chose him.

chapters.title: Day Three
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. With three days until the retainer's date, the third partner dies in a boating accident. Police call it weather. Oscar calls it arithmetic. The beat is racing panic — the countdown is real, and he's watching it tick.

chapters.title: Vivian's Confession, Almost
chapters.summary: Vivian, POV. Vivian nearly tells Oscar everything but instead warns him away, revealing only that Edmund borrowed against the gallery and someone demanded payment. The beat is tragic loyalty — she'd rather lose her husband than her illusion of him.

chapters.title: The Forger's Signature
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. Under raking light, Oscar finds the forged Vermeer bears a hidden monogram — the same mark he saw, as a child, on documents pulled from his parents' burning house. The beat is recognition and horror: the conspiracy and his own history share an author.

chapters.title: The Fourth Name
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. The fourth partner is untraceable — records scrubbed, identity dissolved. Oscar realizes the fourth partner isn't hiding from the killer; the fourth partner is the killer, erasing himself first. The beat is the trap closing: he's hunting a ghost who edits ghosts.

chapters.title: Invisible No More
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. Someone photographs Oscar at the marina and mails the print to his office with a note: 'You remember too much.' His anonymity — his armor — is gone. The beat is exposed vulnerability; the watcher has become the watched.

chapters.title: Edmund's Last Exhibition
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. At the gallery's anniversary show, Oscar watches Edmund say goodbye to patrons like a man settling accounts, and notices the Vermeer has been quietly deaccessioned for 'restoration.' The beat is funereal suspense — the stage is being set for a death everyone will believe.

chapters.title: Day Five: The Empty Frame
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. The forgery vanishes from the vault overnight. Without it, there's no evidence, no motive, no case — only a widowed wife and a drowned partner count rising. The beat is despair at the elegance of the plan: destroy the proof, become innocent.

chapters.title: Memory Is Evidence
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. Oscar realizes his mind is the last copy of the evidence: he has seen the ledger, the monogram, the faces. But memory convicts no one. The beat is bitter resolve — he must force the world to see what only he can remember.

chapters.title: The Drowned Man's Boat
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. Examining the third partner's boat, Oscar finds drill marks in the hull and a paint fleck matching the Ashford boathouse. Edmund didn't just plan his own death — he practiced on his friends. The beat is cold fury replacing fear.

chapters.title: Day Six: Confession at Gunpoint
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. Confronting Edmund in the vault, Oscar recites thirty years of the conspiracy from memory, detail by detail, until Edmund breaks — not with denial, but relief. The beat is the climax's hinge: confession extracted, but no jury will ever hear it.

chapters.title: The Death That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Oscar and Edmund, alternating POV. Edmund stages his disappearance — a fall from the cliff walk — while Oscar watches, holding the evidence that could stop it. The beat is agonizing choice: save the man or keep the proof intact for the living victims.

chapters.title: Vivian's Verdict
chapters.summary: Vivian, POV. Told the whole truth, Vivian learns her marriage, fortune, and the painting were all Edmund's long con — and that he expects her to grieve beautifully, one last performance. She refuses. The beat is quiet, devastating agency: she chooses justice over the role written for her.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV. Unable to use stolen evidence without destroying Vivian, Oscar instead delivers Edmund's confession to the surviving partner's family and lets the underworld do what courts cannot. Edmund vanishes; the conspiracy's debts are collected. The beat is morally gray catharsis — the law failed, so memory became the verdict.

chapters.title: The Perfect Portrait
chapters.summary: Oscar, POV, epilogue. Oscar burns the photograph linking Vivian to the cover-up and files the case closed. Restoring the recovered Vermeer's frame, he finds beneath the gilt a child's chalk drawing — proof that even perfect copies carry the ghost of what they replaced. The beat is bittersweet peace: some things survive forgery, and so, finally, does he.
